extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of architecture and architectural ornament (particularly Byzantine/Venetian)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for observing, interpreting, and judging Byzantine (Venetian) architectural features — especially capitals, archivolts, proportions, and surface ornament — with examples and criteria drawn from St. Mark's and contemporary palaces. Emphasizes subtle proportion, form families, naturalism, and material/color effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minute harmonies of proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular and minute harmonies of proportion (differences of inches on feet) indicate that buildings are of one school and in their original form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurements of arches given (e.g., central archivolt 31'8", adjacent ranges 19'8", 20'4", small flank arches 6'0") are cited as 'irrefragable proof of an intense perception of harmony' by Byzantine architects. Subtle variations, though often undetectable without measurement, influence visual beauty; 'the eye is continually influenced by what it cannot detect.' Compare proportions across examples (apse of Murano, façades, leaf groups) to appreciate this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural features added to consummate proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor architectural elements (e.g. small porticos or flanking arches) may be employed not for utility but solely to consummate the proportions of a façade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two small porticos added at the extremities of a five-door western façade that are 'of no use whatever except to consummate the proportions of the façade.' Observe how such elements complete the rhythm and balance of the main composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan form: central galleries/loggias admitting abundant light
rubrics_metrics.description: Venetian palaces typically present central galleries or loggias opening into apartments on each wing, admitting an immense amount of light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From external fragments one may infer internal disposition: the exterior central arcade relates to interior lighting and circulation. Use presence and scale of arcades/loggias as evidence for original plan and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bold detached shafts and pilaster-assisted supports
rubrics_metrics.description: Central arcades are generally sustained on bold detached cylindrical shafts with rich capitals; wing arches use smaller shafts assisted by wall portions that become pilasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify differences in shaft scale and the transition from free shaft to engaged pilaster as a deliberate compositional device controlling rhythm and visual lightness of façades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two great orders of capitals: convex and concave
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two principal families of capitals: one convex in contour (rich, free fancy) and the other concave (severe, restrained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer models the two families on flower types (water-lily for convex; convolvulus/trumpet for concave). Recognize family membership by overall profile (bulging bell vs. concave sweep) and related ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex (cushion/bell) capital characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Convex family capitals are bold, cushion- or bell-shaped, often derived from a square block rounded into a bell with a simple abacus and richly varied surface decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction sequence (cutting square block's corners, rounding edges, forming bell-stone, adding abacus) yields characteristic silhouette. Look for broad, simple contours supporting varied surface carving; these are 'the Byzantines' favorite' and common in palaces like Murano and St. Mark's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concave (Corinthian-derived) capital characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Concave group capitals are principally founded on the Greek Corinthian, used for nave pillars, often plainer in earliest examples and exhibiting distinct forms in small shaft capitals of palaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure concave profiles sometimes lack decoration except for central incisions; varieties occur where concave forms are cut into arrowy leaf truncations or combined with localized detailing (examples: Fondaco de' Turchi, Casa Farsetti). Use location (nave vs. palace flank) and leaf-treatment to identify subtypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byzantine modification and transitional profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine capitals frequently modify Corinthian concave profiles by bulging out at the bottom, producing transitional forms that combine concave sweeps with convex bells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare profiles: pure concave (needs fillet), pure convex (would be encumbered by fillet), and transitional (concave sweep bending into convex bell at base). These transitions are characteristic of Byzantine adaptation of classical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life: variety and naturalism in ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine capitals display 'Life' — each capital is differently fancied, often with no two sides alike, showing greater love of nature and sketching from real plant forms rather than Greek precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for asymmetric variations, different plant motifs on different faces, individualized birds, and natural gestures (e.g., bunch of grapes, drifting leaves). This vitality is valued over strict classical symmetry and is a mark of 'healthier' or more natural ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth: grand outlines and subordination of detail to mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine sculpture emphasizes excessive breadth: outlines of capitals and leaves are set in grand, simple curves so that minute fretwork is subordinated to a unifying large mould or mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works for dominant sweeping lines and broad surfaces that unify details into a composed whole; this 'unity of perfect ease' links these works to later Italian masters. Note how naturalistic details are enclosed within overarching curves or silhouette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Braided/woven ornament to bind pierced surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Where stone is pierced with minute openings (traceries), intermediate surfaces are carved into interwoven fillets or braided ornament to bind and give unity and repose to the pierced stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize braided work as a response to perforation (starlike openings) — alternately sinking and rising fillets produce unity and often enclose floral motifs; compare to Arab traceries and illuminated manuscript interlace. The braided system is aesthetically and psychologically pleasing due to associations with weaving and hidden unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perforation/traceried reticulation for light and decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute perforations (starlike openings) in stone slabs admit light and air and create delicate internal light patterns; these are often combined with surface ornament for exterior effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe internal lighting effects (stars of light) and external treatment: pierced slabs tend to be given surrounding ornament to avoid a 'scattered and spotty' look — the traceried or reticulated veil both controls light and decorates surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lily capitals: complex braided veil and profiled outlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Lily capitals (St. Mark's) are subtle, complex compositions: a braided or network veil envelops a lily-derived flower on each of the four sides, producing exquisitely varying curvatures and contours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the multiple profiles (inner/outer lines through capital) and how braided work frames the central flower; note the consistent minor motifs (two square/oblong objects at tendril extremities) and the effect of light passing through interstices onto the marble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of bell into lobes with reticulated flower-work
rubrics_metrics.description: Some capitals divide the bell into separate lobes (rose- or tulip-like), each covered with flower-work or hollowed into reticulation, producing more complex three-dimensional silhouettes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify lobed bells by their multi-lobed outline and internal hollowing; examples include capitals from St. Mark's and the central capital of the upper arcade of the Fondaco de' Turchi. These forms yield varied contours from different viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and forms of small wall sculptures above/between archivolts
rubrics_metrics.description: Private palaces often employ small sculptures (crosses, upright oblongs, circles) set in the wall above or between arches; the cross is an invariable ornament usually placed centrally with circular/oblong forms alternating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing façades, note the rhythmic alternation of these small sculptures and their original positions where preserved (St. Mark's, Fondaco de' Turchi). Their arrangement contributes to the overall ornamental grammar of façades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross iconography and its typical central motif
rubrics_metrics.description: The cross placed in palace ornament commonly features, at the meeting of the arms, not a rose but a raised hand in benediction between the sun and moon, signaling theological meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the hand-with-sun-and-moon motif as symbolic of the dependence of heavens and earth upon Redemption; variations exist (sometimes the cross is accompanied only by leaves or doves). Use iconographic reading alongside form analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small sculptural groups of birds and beasts and Mycenaean similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups of birds or beasts (often paired opposite with a small pillar or spray between) are common; these fragments frequently resemble the Lion groups over Mycenae and are reused in later walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe grouping patterns, reuse/reinsertion of fragments, and comparative motifs (e.g., Mycenaean parallels) when assessing originality, dating, and cultural influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesques/contending animals as lower-order ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups of contending and devouring animals are usually more roughly cut and occupy the role of lower grotesques (as in Gothic), offering vigor and variety rather than fine invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the carving quality and purpose: such grotesques provide energetic light-and-shade effects and visual entertainment; they intentionally lack the refined variety of the larger living-leaf capitals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mosaic/gold grounding and colored marbles for contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals and sculptures were often set upon mosaic of gold (or blue in inferior palaces) and veined or colored marbles; a golden reflective ground behind dark traceries produces enchanting alternations of light and shadow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where preserved, note the reflective mosaic in hollows, gilded leaf edges, and bands of color (russet and green) in archivolts; the contrast between pale sculpture and colored/veined backgrounds is a deliberate chromatic device enhancing ornament legibility and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic meanings of common decorative motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many sculptural motifs carry Christian symbolism: the peacock (resurrection), vine (Christ or union with Christ), dove (Holy Spirit), and contending animals (powers of evil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read iconography alongside placement (e.g., cross-centred façades) but avoid overemphasis where uncertain; the prevalence of the cross and certain animals indicates a devotional temper in early Venetian ornamentation.
